stimulus.source_note: Data table from the U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, Historical Poverty Tables, Table 2.
stimulus.text:
| Year | 1959 | 1964 | 1965 | 1966 | 1969 | 1973 |
| Poverty rate | 22.4% | 19.0% | 17.3% | 14.7% | 12.1% | 11.1% |

Official poverty rate, all people. Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, Historical Poverty Tables, Table 2.

stem: The table best supports which conclusion about the timing of the fall in poverty?

options.text: The fastest fall came in the Great Society years
Poverty fell fastest in the 1950s, before the table begins
options.misconception: The table begins in 1959, so it shows nothing about the 1950s before that year.

options.text: Poverty stopped falling once the Great Society ended
options.misconception: The rate keeps falling after 1969, from 12.1 percent to 11.1 percent in 1973.

options.text: Poverty fell by the same amount in every year shown
options.misconception: The drops differ: 2.6 points from 1965 to 1966, but 1.7 points from 1964 to 1965.

rationales.A: The rate drops 6.9 points from 1964 to 1969, the largest fall over any five-year span in the table.
rationales.B: The table starts in 1959, so it cannot show what happened in the 1950s before that year.
rationales.C: The rate falls from 12.1 percent in 1969 to 11.1 percent in 1973, so it kept falling.
rationales.D: The yearly drops differ, so the fall was not the same amount each year.
rationales.general:
1. Work out the falls: 3.4 points from 1959 to 1964, then 6.9 points from 1964 to 1969.
2. The 1964 to 1969 fall is the largest five-year fall in the table.
3. Background: those are the years Johnson's Great Society programs were being passed and put in place.
4. The fastest fall therefore came during the Great Society years.
Remember: The biggest change over time points to the busiest years.
